title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment
summary: At the evening meal before Passover, Jesus rises, takes a towel, and washes his disciples' feet, including Peter's after a protest, and tells them to follow his example. He announces that one of them will betray him, gives the morsel to Judas, and Judas goes out into the night. Jesus then gives the disciples a new commandment to love one another as he has loved them, and warns Peter that he will deny him three times.
story:
With chapter 13 the second half of John's Gospel begins. Jesus' public ministry closed at the end of chapter 12, and for five chapters (13 to 17) the reader is inside a single room on a single night, listening as Jesus prepares his closest followers for his departure. This section is often called the Upper Room Discourse or the Farewell Discourse, though John never mentions an upper room; that detail comes from Mark 14:15 and Luke 22:12. The first verse is a heading for everything that follows: Jesus knew that his hour had come, and “He loved them to the very end.” The foot washing shows that love in action, and the rest of the discourse explains it.

The chapter is also honest about the people who receive that love. Judas, already moved by the devil (13:2), shares the meal, has his feet washed, receives the morsel from Jesus' hand, and goes out into the night. Peter, who protests that he will lay down his life for Jesus, is told that he will deny him three times before morning. The love of verse 1 is given to disciples who will betray, deny, and scatter (16:32), and the new commandment of verse 34 is given to the same people. The rest of the Gospel shows what becomes of them: Judas's story ends in the garden (18:2-5), while Peter's denial is followed by his restoration beside the lake (21:15-19).
historical:
John dates this meal “just before the Passover Feast” (13:1), and later says that the priests would not enter the governor's headquarters so that they could eat the Passover (18:28) and that Jesus was sentenced on the day of Preparation of the Passover (19:14). In Matthew, Mark, and Luke the Last Supper is the Passover meal itself (Mark 14:12-16). How these accounts relate is taken up among the hard questions below. Whatever the answer, John's meal is held at night in Jerusalem during the festival week, when the city was crowded with pilgrims who had come early to purify themselves (11:55).

Two details of the evening reflect Passover custom. When Judas leaves, some disciples assume Jesus has told him to buy what was needed for the feast or to give something to the poor (13:29). Almsgiving at Passover was expected: the Mishnah requires that even the poorest Israelite be given four cups of wine for the Passover meal, from the community's charity fund if necessary (m. Pesahim 10:1). And the warning about the rooster (13:38) may refer to the bird itself or to the Roman watch of the night called cockcrow, roughly midnight to three in the morning; Mark 13:35 names the four watches as evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning. The Mishnah forbids raising chickens in Jerusalem (m. Bava Kamma 7:7), which some interpreters cite in favor of the watch, though the rule's date and enforcement are uncertain and the Gospels speak of an actual crowing (18:27).

The beloved disciple appears here for the first time by that description, reclining next to Jesus (13:23). He reappears at the cross (19:26-27), at the empty tomb (20:2-10), and by the lake (21:7, 21:20-24), where the Gospel names him as the witness behind it but never gives his name. Irenaeus, writing around 180, identified him as John, the disciple who leaned on the Lord's breast and published the Gospel at Ephesus (Against Heresies 3.1.1), and church tradition has taken this to mean John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Many modern scholars accept this. Others note that John's Gospel never names the sons of Zebedee except in 21:2 and that its witness seems at home in Jerusalem, and propose another disciple: Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) and Martin Hengel (The Johannine Question, 1989) argued for John the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple not among the Twelve, while some have suggested Lazarus, whom Jesus is said to love (11:3, 11:5).

Judas is called the son of Simon Iscariot (6:71, 13:2, 13:26), which suggests that Iscariot was a family or place name rather than a nickname. The most common explanation is Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, man of Kerioth, a town in southern Judea (Joshua 15:25), which would make Judas the only Judean among Galilean disciples. Other proposals connect it with the sicarii, the dagger-men who assassinated opponents in Jerusalem in the 50s AD (Josephus, Jewish War 2.254-257), or with an Aramaic word for falsehood; none is certain. John has already told the reader that Judas kept the common purse and stole from it (12:6), and Luke, like John, says that Satan entered him (Luke 22:3).
cultural:
At a formal meal guests reclined on couches or cushions around a low table, leaning on the left elbow with their feet stretched out behind them. That arrangement explains how Jesus could move around the outside of the circle washing feet, and how the beloved disciple, lying to Jesus' right, could lean back against his chest to ask a quiet question (13:25). John's phrase for his place, in the bosom of Jesus (en tō kolpō, 13:23), deliberately echoes 1:18, where the Son is in the bosom of the Father: as the Son makes the Father known, this disciple is placed to make the Son known. Peter was not beside Jesus and had to signal the question across the table (13:24). Judas was near enough to receive a morsel from Jesus' hand.

People walked dusty and muddy roads in sandals, and washing the feet was a basic courtesy of hospitality. Abraham has water brought for his visitors' feet (Genesis 18:4), as do Lot (19:2), Laban's household (24:32), and Joseph's steward (43:24). Normally a host provided water for guests to wash their own feet, or a servant did it. Abigail's offer to wash the feet of David's servants (1 Samuel 25:41) is a gesture of the deepest humility. In the romance Joseph and Aseneth (chapter 20), Aseneth insists on washing Joseph's feet herself rather than letting a maid do it, as a sign of devotion. A rabbinic commentary on Exodus, the Mekilta, discusses the Hebrew slave of Exodus 21:2 and holds that he should not be made to wash his master's feet, a task treated as too degrading for a fellow Israelite and fit for a non-Jewish slave; elsewhere wives, children, or pupils might perform it for a husband, father, or teacher. In every known case the lower serves the higher. John Christopher Thomas (Footwashing in John 13 and the Johannine Community, 1991) gathers this evidence, which shows the task consistently performed by the lower for the higher. That is why Peter is appalled.

Jesus lays aside his outer garments and wraps himself with a towel (lention, from the Latin linteum), the dress of a slave at work. The disciples call him Teacher and Lord (13:13), titles equivalent to rabbi and master. The saying that a messenger is not greater than the one who sent him (13:16) and that whoever receives the one Jesus sends receives Jesus (13:20) reflects a principle later stated in the Mishnah, that a man's agent is like himself (m. Berakhot 5:5).

Sharing bread created a bond of loyalty in the ancient Mediterranean world, so betrayal by one who ate at the same table was especially bitter. Jesus quotes Psalm 41:9, where David laments that a trusted friend who shared his bread has lifted up his heel against him; one of the Thanksgiving Hymns from Qumran (1QHa 13) echoes the same psalm when its speaker laments betrayal by members of his own community. Lifting the heel may picture a kick, a trip, or the insulting gesture of showing the sole of the foot, which remains an insult in much of the Middle East. The morsel (psōmion) was a piece of bread dipped in a common dish. Commentators often suggest that a host offering such a morsel to a guest was paying him a mark of favor. Whether or not that was the custom, Jesus' gesture comes as an offer of friendship to the man he knows will betray him.
literary:
The chapter moves from action to meaning, and it is built in five movements. The opening sentence (13:1) is long and solemn: it gathers the hour, the Passover, the departure to the Father, and the love Jesus had for his own, and it serves as a heading for the whole second half of the Gospel. The phrase to the very end (eis telos) carries a double sense, to the end of his life and to the uttermost degree, and it anticipates Jesus' last word from the cross, It is finished (tetelestai, 19:30).

The foot washing (13:1-11) is an acted parable, and Jesus explains it twice: first to Peter as a cleansing without which he has no part with Jesus (13:8), then to all as an example of humble service (13:12-17). Some scholars have seen two layers of tradition in these explanations. Many recent interpreters, among them John Christopher Thomas and Mary Coloe (in her study Welcome into the Household of God), read the two as intended together, the first grounding the second: only those whom Jesus has washed can wash others. John's verbs for Jesus laying aside his garments (tithēsin, 13:4) and taking them again (elaben, 13:12) are the verbs of the Good Shepherd who lays down his life and takes it up again (10:17-18), so the scene quietly points to the cross.

The account of the betrayal (13:18-30) is framed by knowledge. Jesus knows whom he has chosen (13:18); he tells them in advance “so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He” (13:19). The Greek is simply I am (egō eimi), echoing the Greek of Isaiah 43:10, where the Lord calls Israel to know and believe that I am. The scene ends with one of the most loaded short sentences in the Gospel: Judas “went out into the night” (13:30). In John night is more than a time; it is the darkness that the light came to overcome (1:5, 3:2, 9:4, 11:10).

The last section (13:31-38) opens the discourse proper. The moment Judas leaves, Jesus says that the Son of Man is glorified, using the verb glorify five times in two verses (13:31-32). He addresses the disciples as little children (teknia), the only time in the Gospel, though the word is frequent in 1 John. Then comes the new commandment (13:34-35) set between two announcements of departure (13:33, 13:36). The chapter ends not with the commandment but with Peter's bold promise and Jesus' sober reply, so that the command to love is framed by betrayal on one side and denial on the other.

outline.t: Jesus foretells the betrayal; Judas goes out

doctrines.note: The chapter opens with Jesus loving his own to the very end (13:1) and closes with the new commandment: “As I have loved you, so you also must love one another” (13:34). The command to love one's neighbor was old (Leviticus 19:18); what is new is its measure, the self-giving love of Jesus, and its role as the visible mark of his community: “By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another” (13:35).

“Whoever has already bathed needs only to wash his feet, and he will be completely clean” (13:10). Many readers since Augustine have taken this to mean that those made clean through Christ still need ongoing cleansing from daily sin, a reading that fits 1 John 1:7-9. Others read the washing as a single picture of the cleansing Jesus' death accomplishes. Either way, the disciple must receive before he can serve (13:8).

Jesus, whom the disciples rightly call Teacher and Lord, takes the place of a slave and tells them to do as he has done (13:13-15). The chapter sets the pattern for authority among his followers: those who lead are servants, and no messenger is greater than the one who sent him (13:16). Luke places the dispute about greatness at the same supper (Luke 22:24-27).

Some Christian traditions, including Mennonites and other Anabaptists, the Church of the Brethren, Free Will and Primitive Baptists, and Seventh-day Adventists, practice foot washing as an ordinance because of 13:14-15. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and Lutheran churches keep it as a rite on Maundy Thursday, and most Protestant churches treat it as an example of humble service rather than a commanded rite. This is a second-order difference among faithful churches.

As soon as Judas goes out to betray him, Jesus says, “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him” (13:31). The betrayal sets in motion the hour of the cross, which John treats as the place where the Father and the Son are glorified in each other. The glory is revealed not in escaping betrayal but in going through it.

words.note: Telos, end, goal, completion. It occurs about 40 times in the New Testament and only here in John, in the phrase eis telos (13:1). The phrase can mean to the end, of time, or to the uttermost, of degree, and John likely intends both: Jesus loved his own to the last hour of his life and to the fullest extent. The related verb teleō appears when Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, says It is finished (19:28, 19:30).

Niptō, to wash part of the body, such as the hands, face, or feet. It occurs 17 times in the New Testament and eight times in this chapter. In 13:10 John sets it beside louō, to bathe the whole body: the one who has bathed (leloumenos) needs only to wash his feet. The distinction lets Jesus answer Peter, who swings from refusing to be washed at all to asking to be washed all over. Commentators disagree whether the bathing refers to baptism, to the cleansing word Jesus has spoken (15:3), or simply to the disciples' fundamental cleanness through him.

Meros, part, share, portion. It occurs about 42 times in the New Testament. To have a part with someone (13:8) is to share in his lot and inheritance, a phrase with Old Testament roots in the portion of land each tribe received and the Levites' portion, which was the Lord himself (Numbers 18:20, Deuteronomy 12:12). Jesus tells Peter that without being washed by him he has no share in what Jesus is and will receive. The foot washing is not only an example; it is something only Jesus can do for a disciple.

Hypodeigma, example, pattern, model. It occurs six times in the New Testament (John 13:15; Hebrews 4:11, 8:5, 9:23; James 5:10; 2 Peter 2:6). Jesus says, “I have set you an example” (13:15). BDAG describes it as a model or pattern to be imitated or, in a negative sense, a warning. Here it means a pattern the disciples must reproduce in their own service, not merely an illustration of humility; whether it requires the literal act of foot washing is the question that divides the churches.

Paradidōmi, to hand over, deliver, betray. It occurs about 119 times in the New Testament and some 15 times in John. The same verb can describe handing on a tradition (1 Corinthians 11:23), God's giving up of his Son (Romans 8:32), Jesus' giving up of his spirit on the cross (John 19:30), and Judas's betrayal (13:2, 13:11, 13:21). In John, Judas is introduced again and again as the one who would hand him over, so that his name becomes inseparable from the act.

Psōmion, a morsel, a small piece of bread. It occurs only in this passage in the New Testament (13:26 twice, 13:27, 13:30). The word marks the moment of decision: Jesus dips the morsel and gives it to Judas, Satan enters Judas as he takes it, and as soon as he has received it he goes out. The repetition of the word four times slows the narrative to a single gesture of offered friendship that is received and refused.

Kainos, new, fresh, of a new kind. It occurs about 42 times in the New Testament. The command to love one's neighbor was old (Leviticus 19:18), and 1 John 2:7-8 plays on the command being both old and new. What is new here is its measure (as I have loved you), its setting on the night of Jesus' self-giving, and the community it creates. Kainos often describes the new things of God's promised age, the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31, Luke 22:20) and the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), but the link to covenant in this verse is thematic, not stated.

Agapaō, to love. It occurs about 143 times in the New Testament and some 37 times in John, six of them in this chapter. The Gospel opens this half with Jesus loving his own to the end (13:1), introduces the disciple whom Jesus loved (13:23), and closes the scene with the command to love as he loved (13:34-35). Some older preaching drew a sharp contrast between agapaō and phileō, but John uses both of the Father's love for the Son (3:35, 5:20) and of Jesus' love for Lazarus (11:3, 11:5), so the distinction should not be pressed.

christ:
In washing feet, Jesus acts out what Paul would later put into words in Philippians 2:5-8: the one who was in the form of God took the form of a servant and humbled himself to the point of death on a cross. John prepares the act with a sentence about Jesus' supreme status: he knew that the Father had put all things into his hands and that he had come from God and was returning to God (13:3). His humility is not a lack of status but the use of supreme status for others. The Servant of Isaiah, who pours out his life and bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), stands in the background, and Luke records the saying at the same meal that Jesus is among them as one who serves (Luke 22:27).

The foot washing points to the cross. Without it, no one has a part with him (13:8), and the cleansing it pictures is the cleansing his death accomplishes (1 John 1:7). Jesus also goes to his death knowingly. He knows the hour, knows the Father's gift, knows the betrayer, and tells the disciples in advance so that when it happens they will believe that I am (13:19), the divine self-designation of Isaiah 43:10. The betrayal does not catch him unawares. It fulfills the pattern of the righteous sufferer of Psalm 41, whose trusted friend turned against him, and Jesus meets it with the offer of the morsel.

When Judas has gone out, Jesus speaks of glory (13:31-32). The cross is the place where God is glorified in the Son and the Son in God. And the new commandment makes Jesus' own love the standard for his people. The church's life together is meant to be a visible continuation of the love that washed feet and went to the cross, so that the world recognizes Jesus in his disciples (13:35). Finally, the warning to Peter shows a Lord who knows the weakness of his friends and loves them anyway; the one who foretells the denial will also restore the one who denied (21:15-19).
interpretation:
The church read the foot washing both as an example and as a mystery from early on. In northern Italy, Gaul, and parts of Spain the newly baptized had their feet washed as they came from the font. The Council of Elvira in Spain, in the early fourth century, forbade priests and clergy to perform this washing (canon 48), and Rome did not practice it, but Ambrose of Milan defended the custom and treated it as a sacrament in its own right, instituted by Christ for Peter (On the Sacraments, book 3). Augustine's Tractates on John 55 to 66 cover the chapter; he read the washing of feet as Christ's daily cleansing of the sins that cling to those already bathed in baptism, and he tied the new commandment to the new song and new people of the new covenant. John Chrysostom (Homilies 70 to 72 on John) marveled that Jesus washed the feet of Judas and used the scene to rebuke pride. Bernard of Clairvaux, in a sermon for the Lord's Supper, spoke of the foot washing as a sacrament for the remission of daily sins.

In the Western liturgy the washing became the Mandatum of Holy Thursday, named from the Latin of verse 34, mandatum novum, a new commandment, and the English name Maundy Thursday comes from the same word. The hymn Ubi caritas, where charity and love are, there God is, has long been sung during the rite. English monarchs once washed the feet of poor people on that day; the Royal Maundy survives as a distribution of coins. In 2013 Pope Francis washed the feet of young inmates at the Casal del Marmo detention center in Rome, including two women and two Muslims, and a decree of 2016 opened the rite to women and girls. The Revised Common Lectionary reads 13:1-17 and 31b-35 on Maundy Thursday every year, and 13:31-35 on the fifth Sunday of Easter in Year C.

The Reformers treated the washing as an example, not a sacrament. John Calvin's commentary argued that Christ commanded the humility the act expressed, not an annual ceremony, and he criticized the annual ceremony of his day as a theatrical imitation that missed the point. The Anabaptist tradition took the command literally. The Mennonite Dordrecht Confession of 1632 (article 11) confesses foot washing as instituted and commanded by Christ, a sign of humility and a reminder of the true washing by his blood, and the practice continues among Mennonites, Brethren, several Baptist bodies, and Seventh-day Adventists, who call it the ordinance of humility. Modern study has asked what the act meant in its ancient setting (John Christopher Thomas, 1991) and how the two explanations in verses 6 to 11 and 12 to 17 relate.

Judas has a long history of his own. Dante put him in the lowest circle of hell, in the central mouth of Satan (Inferno, canto 34). A second-century Gnostic text known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.31.1), the Gospel of Judas, recast him as the one disciple who understood Jesus; a Coptic copy in Codex Tchacos was published by the National Geographic Society in 2006. Jorge Luis Borges played with similar ideas in his story Three Versions of Judas (1944). Karl Barth gave Judas an extended treatment in Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942), within his doctrine of election, as the rejected one for whom Christ was himself rejected. Jewish scholars, among them Hyam Maccoby (Judas Iscariot and the Myth of Jewish Evil, 1992), have traced how Judas, whose name echoes Judah, was used in Christian polemic as a symbol of the Jewish people, a use the text does not support.

In art, Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper in Milan (1495 to 1498) captures the moment of the announcement that one of you will betray me (13:21, and its parallels), as the disciples turn to one another. Tintoretto painted The Washing of the Feet several times, including the large canvas of about 1548 to 1549 now in the Prado, and Ford Madox Brown's Jesus Washing Peter's Feet (1852 to 1856, Tate) shows Jesus kneeling in a plain workman's posture while Peter sits in embarrassment.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 2 the best manuscripts read a present participle, while supper was taking place (deipnou ginomenou), which modern versions render during supper or the evening meal was underway; later manuscripts read an aorist (genomenou), which the King James Version renders ‘supper being ended’, though the story shows the meal still going on (13:26). In the same verse the older text can be read, literally, the devil had already put it into the heart that Judas son of Simon Iscariot should betray him, which some commentators take to mean that the devil had made up his own mind; the later text makes the heart Judas's (‘into the heart of Judas’, KJV). Modern versions generally follow the sense of the later reading.

In verse 10 a few witnesses, most notably Codex Sinaiticus, omit except the feet, giving the saying ‘whoever has bathed has no need to wash, but is clean all over’. Some scholars have preferred this shorter text and read the washing as a single, complete cleansing. Most editions keep the longer text, which has the stronger manuscript support, and suspect that scribes dropped the phrase because it seemed to sit awkwardly with completely clean. In verse 18 the best manuscripts quote Psalm 41:9 as the one who eats my bread, while others read eats bread with me, closer to the psalm and to Mark 14:18. In verse 32 the opening clause, If God is glorified in Him, is missing from several early manuscripts and was omitted by Westcott and Hort; it may have fallen out because the eye skipped between the repeated words, and modern editions print it, some in brackets.

There are also translation differences. The KJV's ‘Master and Lord’ in verses 13 and 14 renders the same word the BSB translates Teacher. In verse 23 the KJV's ‘leaning on Jesus' bosom’ is literal; modern versions render the idiom as reclining at his side or next to him. In verse 34 the BSB, like most versions, translates the purpose clause as a command, so you also must love one another.

teach.big: Jesus, knowing his full authority and his coming death, loves his own to the end by taking a slave's place, and he calls his disciples, who will fail him, to receive his cleansing and to love one another in the same way.

outline.t: Jesus' humility flows from security, not insecurity: because he knows who he is and where he is going, he is free to kneel.
Before we can serve like Jesus we must let him serve us; pride can take the form of refusing to be washed.
The servant Lord gives an example, and blessing comes from doing it, not merely knowing it.
Betrayal does not catch Jesus by surprise; his foreknowledge is meant to strengthen faith that he is the I am.
Jesus is troubled by betrayal and still offers friendship to the betrayer; Judas's going out into the night shows the terrible freedom to refuse love.
The new commandment makes Jesus' own love the measure and mark of his people, visible to everyone.
Jesus knows our weakness better than we do, and his prediction of Peter's failure is not the end of Peter's story.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first reduces the foot washing to a lesson in good manners or generic niceness. Jesus' act is a slave's task done by the Lord, it pictures a cleansing without which no one belongs to him (13:8), and it points to the cross. The second makes it only a sacrament or only an example; the chapter gives both explanations, and teachers should hold them together. The third turns the passage into an argument about whether churches must practice literal foot washing. That is a legitimate question on which churches differ, but it should not crowd out the humility the act calls for.

With Judas, avoid two opposite errors. One makes him a mere pawn with no choice, which the text resists by showing Jesus' repeated warnings and offer of the morsel. The other makes him uniquely monstrous, a figure on whom others can project evil, as happened when Christian polemic used him as a symbol of the Jewish people. The Gospel's point is that betrayal can come from inside the circle, and every disciple is asked, in Mark's version, Is it I?

With the new commandment, avoid defining love as agreeable feeling or tolerance of anything. The measure is Jesus' love, which washes feet, tells the truth, and lays down life. Avoid also pitting love against truth or doctrine; John's letters hold them together (1 John 3:18). Finally, do not preach Peter's denial as proof that Peter was a coward and we would do better. Every disciple at the table scattered (16:32).
teach.pastoral: The chapter touches people who have been betrayed by someone close, a friend, a spouse, a church leader. Jesus' own distress at the betrayal (13:21) shows that betrayal wounds even the Son of God; it is not a failure of faith to be troubled by it. Teach the command to serve with care in a room that includes people who have been exploited or abused. Humble service is freely given love, not submission to mistreatment, and Jesus' example never requires anyone to remain under abuse. Some hearers are scrupulous, afraid that any sin since conversion has undone their cleansing; Jesus' words that the bathed person needs only to wash the feet can reassure them. Others carry the shame of having denied their faith or failed someone at a decisive moment; point them forward to Peter's restoration in chapter 21.

hard.q: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal, as the other Gospels say, or did it happen the day before, as John seems to say?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. Matthew, Mark, and Luke describe the Last Supper as a Passover meal, prepared on the day the lambs were sacrificed (Mark 14:12-16), so that Jesus died on the afternoon of Passover day itself. John places the supper before the feast (13:1), has the priests still waiting to eat the Passover on the morning of the trial (18:28), and says Jesus was sentenced on the day of Preparation of the Passover at about noon (19:14), about the hour the lambs began to be slaughtered. Bart Ehrman (Jesus, Interrupted, 2009) and many critical scholars conclude that the accounts cannot both be right and that John changed the date to present Jesus as the Passover lamb (compare 1:29, 19:36).

The responses fall into four groups. Some hold that the Synoptic chronology is historical and John's is theological; Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) argued at length that the meal had the marks of a Passover. Others hold the reverse: Raymond Brown and John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 1, 1991) judged John's dating more likely and thought the Synoptic writers presented a farewell meal in Passover terms. A third group proposes different calendars. Annie Jaubert (La date de la Cène, 1957) argued that Jesus followed the solar calendar known from Jubilees and Qumran and ate the Passover on Tuesday evening, while the temple followed the official calendar, and Colin Humphreys (The Mystery of the Last Supper, 2011) argued for a Wednesday meal on an older calendar reckoning. A fourth group argues that the accounts agree once John's terms are read in their festival sense: D. A. Carson (1991) and Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of John's Gospel, 2001) take eating the Passover in 18:28 to refer to the festival meals that followed the Passover proper, and the day of Preparation of the Passover in 19:14 to mean the Friday of Passover week, the day before the Sabbath (as 19:31 and 19:42 use the word).

None of these proposals has settled the question, and faithful readers hold each of them. What all four Gospels agree on is that Jesus died at Passover, in the setting of Israel's great feast of deliverance, and that his death was the fulfillment of what that feast signified; Paul, writing earlier than any of the Gospels, already calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

hard.q: If Scripture had to be fulfilled and Satan entered Judas, was Judas really responsible?
hard.a:
The objection runs like this. Jesus says the betrayal fulfills Psalm 41:9 (13:18), the devil has already put the betrayal into Judas's heart (13:2), and Satan enters him the moment he takes the morsel (13:27). Jesus even tells him to act quickly. If the outcome was foretold, foreknown, and driven by Satan, Judas looks less like a traitor than a pawn. The Gnostic Gospel of Judas, from the second century, went further and made him the one disciple who carried out Jesus' true wishes, and modern writers from Borges (Three Versions of Judas, 1944) onward have explored whether Judas was a necessary instrument who deserved pity rather than blame. Hyam Maccoby (Judas Iscariot and the Myth of Jewish Evil, 1992) argued from a Jewish perspective that the figure of Judas grew in the telling as the church sought someone to blame.

The main responses draw on the text itself. John Chrysostom (Homilies on John 70 to 72) stressed that Jesus warned Judas repeatedly, washed his feet, and offered him the morsel, all of which were invitations to turn back; foreknowledge, on this view, does not cause what it foresees. Augustine distinguished God's permission and use of evil from the evil will of the one who commits it. The Gospel itself gives Judas a motive of his own, greed (12:6), and the other Gospels record a price and remorse (Matthew 26:14-16, 27:3-5). Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942) placed Judas within the mystery of election, as one whose rejection Christ himself bore, while insisting that his act was real treachery. Calvinist and Arminian readers differ on how God's purpose relates to Judas's choice, as they differ elsewhere.

What John will not do is make Judas a mere mechanism. The narrative shows a disciple who shared the table, received love, and went out into the night by his own act. It also refuses to make him a scapegoat: Jesus announces the betrayal while every disciple wonders whether he is the one.

observe: What does verse 3 say Jesus knew, and what does he do in verses 4 and 5 because of it?
How does Peter respond at each stage of the foot washing, and how does Jesus answer him?
What is new about the commandment in verse 34, and what will it show everyone according to verse 35?
interpret: Why does Jesus say that unless he washes Peter, Peter has no part with him? What does that suggest the foot washing means beyond an example?
Why do you think John records that Judas went out, and adds that it was night?
How does Peter's promise to lay down his life relate to what Jesus is about to do for him?
apply: Is it harder for you to receive humble love or to give it? What does Peter's reaction suggest about why?
Jesus washed Judas's feet too. Whose feet would it be hardest for you to wash, and what would that look like in practice?
If people judged Jesus' followers only by their love for one another, what would they conclude about your church?
